claims.text: An integrated framework combining harmonic and anharmonic lattice-vibration modeling with machine-learning regression can accurately predict low phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed framework will reduce prediction error by at least 20% relative to conventional models.
Equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn and its compositional derivatives can be prepared with well-controlled microstructures through consistent annealing and quenching.
Ab initio lattice dynamics can be supplemented with explicit anharmonic corrections obtained from molecular dynamics or advanced perturbative methods.
Machine-learning regression can be trained on calculated local vibrational modes and phonon-scattering data.
Local lattice distortions and configurational disorder enhance phonon scattering in high-entropy alloys.
Anharmonic vibrational effects further enhance phonon scattering at elevated temperatures.
Chemical complexity and atomic-scale disorder induce significant local lattice distortions and mass-fluctuation effects in high-entropy alloys.
Local lattice distortions and mass fluctuations create strong phonon-scattering centers.
Combining anharmonicity-corrected DFT with machine learning can capture both harmonic and anharmonic contributions to phonon transport.
The integrated framework can capture anisotropic vibrational interactions neglected by standard methods.
Existing prediction methods typically rely on harmonic approximations and empirical models.
Existing prediction methods omit full anharmonic treatment and complex scattering interactions in disordered systems.
The framework is applicable when phonon scattering is dominated by chemical disorder and anharmonic vibrational interactions.
Extreme anharmonicity may limit the framework's applicability.
Magnetic ordering or other dominant effects may invalidate vibrational scattering as the primary predictive descriptor.
The effectiveness of the machine-learning component depends on the availability and quality of high-fidelity training data.
TDTR measurements over 300 K to 1073 K can benchmark predicted phonon thermal conductivity for systematically varied high-entropy alloys.
Failure to reduce prediction error by at least 20% relative to current approaches would falsify the hypothesis.
Achieving accurate predictions only for high-entropy alloys with minimal mass contrast would falsify the hypothesis.
